course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 1
unit.description: Follow Native American societies, European exploration, the Columbian Exchange, and the Spanish empire from 1491 to 1607.

topics.title: Contextualizing Period 1
topics.summary: What a historical context is, and the Native American, European, and African developments that framed the encounters of 1491 to 1607.

topics.title: Native American Societies Before European Contact
topics.summary: How maize, aridity, mixed farming, and ocean resources shaped the economies and settlements of Native American societies across North America before 1491.

topics.title: European Exploration in the Americas
topics.summary: Why Spain, Portugal, England, and France sent ships across the Atlantic: wealth, rivalry among monarchies, and the spread of Christianity.

topics.title: Columbian Exchange, Spanish Exploration, and Conquest
topics.summary: What crossed the Atlantic after 1492, how epidemics and alliances made Spanish conquest possible, and how American silver and new business methods changed Europe's economy.

topics.title: Labor, Slavery, and Caste in the Spanish Colonial System
topics.summary: How the encomienda, African slavery, and the casta system organized work and social rank across the Spanish empire in the Americas.

topics.title: Cultural Interactions Between Europeans, Native Americans, and Africans
topics.summary: How Europeans, Native Americans, and Africans misunderstood and borrowed from one another, how Native peoples defended their lands, and how Spanish leaders argued over the treatment of Native peoples.

topics.title: Causation in Period 1
topics.summary: How to explain the causes and effects of the transatlantic voyages of 1491–1607: separating long-term and short-term causes, tracing chains of effects, and weighing competing explanations.
